title: And it stars Stephen Spinella, Tony-winning star of the original Ange...
transcript: an old gay throuple is the subject matter of this new play and it's one of my favorite shows of the year so far. taking place in an Arizona ghost town in 1992 an old gay couple after being together for 28 years invites a new person into their relationship but tensions between them rise when one of them faces rapidly declining health and the mysterious newcomer confronts his old demons. play is called Jerome, by John J. Caswell Jr., who broke onto the scene a couple years ago in a big way with two extremely weird plays Wet Brain and Scene Partners and this one isn't quite as weird but still leaves a lot to chew on. from the moment it begins I was so utterly invested in the profound love and commitment between these two older men. even when the third enters the scene I completely bought into the dynamic a testament to the sharp writing, direction, and acting which infuses this kind of titillating, novel subject matter with so much warmth and tenderness that carries it through the rest of the play. but even before the characters come into conflict with each other we know and feel that all is not necessarily well this is the height of the AlDS epidemic after all so even as they've managed to escape into a sort of self-made haven and even as they fight to make the most of this just life they've built together the world outside still looms large and we feel that especially in Dustin Wills’s surprisingly tech-heavy production with a lot of striking imagery: an eerie light-up Christmas tree on the fritz a rock face with a single weed growing out of it and even some other surprises in the staging that I won't spoil. all of which creates this undercurrent of unease like they're haunted by the cosmic and natural forces that rage outside their door. I will say Act 2 loses some of the precision and momentum they had in Act 1 and also, maybe it's just my past experience with Caswell's work but it felt like they were flirting with the surreal; kind of teasing a more audaciously weird twist that never quite came and it didn't bother me that much but I do think the little hints of heightened reality that we do get don't feel as satisfying or effective as they might have otherwise but for me the play sticks the landing and still ended up gripping me from beginning to end
